utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there are no preliminaries. Therefore, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue the cross-examination, I would like to remind you that you are -- no, the examination, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if you're ready, you may proceed. I do understand that you have one hour after 15 minutes left at least of the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, that's correct. I will try to complete in my time, I hope to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. When we left off we were talking about the 13 July 1995, the events of that day, and we spoke about the morning. Now I'd like to ask you about any trips you made that day along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. Did you travel that road on the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you came to travel that road the first time, where you went and why you set off down the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, after returning from Potocari, I went to the Bratunac Brigade military police headquarters, and in a conversation with Mirko Jankovic, the police commander, I learned that on that day, on that road, General Mladic was supposed to pass with his entourage. The reason I went there was of a military nature because on the 13th already, all the activities were taking place other than the transportation of civilians from Potocari, so all the military activities were in place on that communication. They were happening there. As the chief of security and intelligence, it was my duty, among other things, to provide security for the commander of the Main Staff or any other superior command, or any superior officer from one of these two commands. So it was my duty to provide additional escorts and take care of security of the officer who was in the area of responsibility of my unit. I went to this communication to check whether the road was passable and how secure it was, and everything that had to do with security on that road. That was the only reason why I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And about what time, approximately, did you drive down the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, the first time, I'm speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the closest that I can still recall about the times and I always had to reiterate that I cannot really be absolutely precise, but I would say that I was travelling down that road sometime before 12.00 or perhaps after 12.00 but basically that was the time frame when I was travelling down that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on the way to Konjevic Polje from Bratunac, did you see any prisoners or any Muslim men? Put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I travelled down there, in the Sandici sector, I saw a group of Muslims who had surrendered or had been taken prisoners, I'm really am not sure but they were there, at the point where -- at the place where some of the officers from the special MUP brigade were, that brigade, that unit was headed by Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the name of any officers or MUP officers you saw there at Sandici?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Sandici, I saw members of the special MUP brigade because they were easily identifiable. Of those that I saw myself, there was Ljubisa Borovcanin, he was the deputy commander of the special MUP brigade, and, of course, in this area, in other words the parts where the police forces were engaged, that was where their engagement began. From Sandici all the way to Konjevic Polje, there were different police units that were engaged, in other words special purpose units, special brigade members, members of the Jahorina units and so on, but what's important to say is that there were police forces engaged between Sandici and Konjevic Polje. They were easy to recognise because they had -- the special MUP brigade had heavy weaponry, they had APCs, and of course I saw their commander there who was commanding all the forces that were engaged in that -- on that axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on this trip, did you have any contact with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in the afternoon, I was there waiting for General Mladic to pass, and General Mladic came to Konjevic Polje with his personal security. There was a department from the military police of the Bratunac Brigade there. I met them at the crossroads in Konjevic Polje, and Mladic stopped, his car parked, and he got out. I went up to him and I submitted my report. Basically I said that everything was okay on that communication, that everything had been taken care, so basically this was just -- I submitted my military report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters are kindly requesting that the witness slows down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, could you please slow down your speech so that we don't miss any of your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were there any prisoners present at Konjevic Polje at this time when you made your report to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were already prisoners there in Konjevic Polje. This was already in the afternoon hours on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said that you spoke to General Mladic. Did you notice if General Mladic spoke to the prisoners at all, addressed them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic got out of his vehicle, he -- the vehicle was parked, together with his escorts, on the opposite side if you're coming from Bratunac, outside an old yellow-walled building. It was a co-op of some sort, an agricultural kind of building or facility. General Mladic moved back towards Bratunac and on a field viewing from Bratunac, there was, on the right-hand side, a group of prisoners. General Mladic said that everything would be all right, that they shouldn't have any concerns, they shouldn't be worried, and that after that on that same day after a while they would be taken wherever they chose. So this was -- he did address them verbally, this group that was standing there. It wasn't a large group but it was already there in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after that, did you speak to General Mladic? Did you have any conversation with him, after he addressed those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the time while General Mladic was in Konjevic Polje, in other words since his arrival and the moment that I briefed him and all that time while he was there, I was about a metre behind him or I was next to him, on his -- at his side. He stayed there briefly and when he said this, that these prisoners would be all right, that nothing would happen to them, that they would be taken wherever they chose, he turned around and headed towards the vehicles that were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is supposed to remain seated and I do understand that he would like to consult with you, Mr. Petrusic. You have -- if it can be limited to 30 seconds, it may be done but only at very low voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Low voice, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, it should not be audible anywhere else in this courtroom. Mr. Nikolic did you hear any words spoken by Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, sorry for that short interruption. You were just -- if you could finish your answer, you just said: "... when he said this that these prisoners would be all right, that nothing would happen to them, that they would be taken wherever they chose, he turned around and headed towards the vehicles that were --" So if you could continue and, again, my question was if you had any conversation with General Mladic after he had addressed the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will continue from where I left off. General Mladic headed towards the vehicles that were there, his own vehicle and the escort vehicle, and then I asked him -- I was walking next to him and I asked him, General, what will really happen to these people? Because I would like to say it here and now, even then I didn't believe that they would go whatever they wanted to, and of course today I know -- I didn't believe it then and of course today I know what happened to them. He, General Mladic, smiled, he didn't say anything, he didn't make any comments, he just made a gesture with his hand, with his arm like this, and he went into the car and continued on his way. This is what happened after he addressed the prisoners and before he left the Konjevic Polje sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We couldn't see the gesture you were referring to. What was the gesture General Mladic made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He made a gesture, he sort of moved his arm and hand from left to right, he smiled, and -- he laughed, and he went into the car and left for Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the transcript, the witness approximately at the middle of his body made a movement right hand going from left to right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after that conversation with General Mladic, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After General Mladic left together with his entourage, I was approached by members of the civilian police. They came up to me and said that in a facility in Konjevic Polje, as far as I can recall this was a facility that housed members of the 5th Engineering Battalion of the Drina Corps, they told me that they had a very important prisoner held in that facility. They told me the name of this person, his name was Resid Sinanovic, and of course I knew who this prisoner was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, how did you know who Mr. Resid Sinanovic was? If you could just explain how you knew him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Resid Sinanovic personally. He lived and worked in Bratunac, as I did. He was a bit older than I was but I knew both him and his entire family. Before the war, he was a prominent man. He was a chief of police, and that is a prominent post in a town. And in addition to that, he also worked for a large company in Bratunac called Kaolin. He was one of the directors in the legal department. But what was so special about him and what was so important about him was the fact that before the war he was the chief of the public security station in Bratunac, and that's why everyone knew him and I knew him, too, privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then what happened? What did you do with Mr. Sinanovic or did you see Mr. Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took Resid Sinanovic with me. He was in the vehicle while I was driving to Konjevic Polje, and there was a member of the Bratunac Brigade military police, so he and I, we took over this prisoner, Resid Sinanovic, and took him to the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac, and the military police, and I personally handed him over to Zlatan Celanovic, who was our lawyer, and he was in charge of questioning prisoners of war, people who escaped or fled from various areas, and people who were subject to questioning. I must say here, because I've already mentioned that he was an important man, and I want to explain why it was that I took him over and why he was considered an important prisoner. There was indicia that Sinanovic, Resid, had committed some war crimes during the war. He was on the MUP lists as one of the war criminals, and in Bjelovac and in that area where his parents otherwise lived and he also had a property there were indications that he had committed a war crime. So I took him over and handed him over to a military police organ so that they would establish the truth, whether there was any evidence for that, and this is why he was taken prisoner and identified as an important prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did Zlatan Celanovic ever tell you the results of his interrogation or conversation with Resid Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On every occasion, including this time, Zlatan Celanovic told, or rather, submitted reports to the commander and to me as well on the questioning of each and every prisoner. Celanovic also told me in person, perhaps on that same day in the afternoon or on the following day, that during the questioning and by comparing all the reports that he had received previously from the prisoners from Srebrenica, that there were no grounds for this and that in his view there was -- there were no grounds for submitting any criminal report against Resid Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And briefly, if you know, can you tell us what happened to Mr. Sinanovic following his interrogation by Mr. Celanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you only what Mr. Celanovic told me. After the question -- after the interrogation, and after he was visited by some friends and acquaintances, Serbs who had worked with him together with Mr. Sinanovic, he moved him to the Vuk Karadzic elementary school on his own initiative, and kept him there with the other prisoners who had already been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then very briefly, if you can very briefly, if you know, what was Mr. -- what happened to Mr. Sinanovic after being taken to the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with the other prisoners, on the 14th of July, in the morning, he was transferred to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, and according to what I learned and the information that I have, Resid Sinanovic was executed together with the other prisoners who had been taken to Zvornik. He wasn't killed, he was injured. He had severe injuries, and injured as he was he swam across the river and got into Serbia in Banja Koviljaca. In other words he moved, he swam across the river from Bosnia into Serbia and found himself in Banja Koviljaca. People recognised him there because he frequently travelled that -- along that route, and he frequently went to a cafe there. So people recognised him and they transferred him to a hospital. He stayed in the hospital for a while, he was then transferred to Loznica, and he was recognised in this hospital by a doctor, a neighbour of his who lived in the same building before the war where he did. They lived on the same floor in an apartment building. She informed the Bratunac MUP. And now I just assume based on the information that I have that the Bratunac MUP informed the Zvornik police who took him over, they took him out of the hospital, and Resid Sinanovic was liquidated on the bridge on the Drina River somewhere in the sector of Zvornik on the way from Serbia to Bosnia, the bridge spanning the two republics. And just to provide all the information, I have to say that my Defence counsel researched all the documents from the hospital and the events surrounding this case, and they handed over these documents to the OTP before my first trial here. In other words, all the documents that dealt with his transfer to the hospital, his stay in the hospital, his medical records there and everything else to do with that. Now, the information that I'm now providing and what I'm saying here is that this doctor from Bratunac informed the police, and this information I learned from my Defence counsel, Londrovic and Kirsch, after they had done this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on, did you make another journey down the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road later that same day, 13 July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did go one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you and just ask, can you tell us who you went with and what vehicle you went in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went the same day in the afternoon with the commander of the military police, Mirko Jankovic, and the deputy commander of the Bratunac Brigade military police, Milo Petrovic, and we went in an APC of the UNPROFOR, or rather, of the DutchBat, because during that day and earlier in the Bratunac Brigade we did have a few APCs available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you just tell us where you went down that road and if you had any contacts with Muslim men that day as you went down the road?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went along the same route as the first day, the Bratunac-Kravica-Sandici-Pervani-Lolici-Konjevic Polje route. And if I can remember, after we passed Pervani or Lolici we caught up with a group of six Muslim men, then - this was the second time that I went along this road - there were already -- there were already many men who had surrendered or were captured, starting from Sandici all the way to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did that -- thank you. Did the APC have a loud speaker system and if it did was it used during this trip?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the APCs including the one that we used had a megaphone as part of its equipment. Mile Petrovic from Sandici, when we got to Sandici, from time to time used the megaphone calling on the Muslims to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, a moment ago you said that you - and by you, I mean you and Mirko Jankovic and his deputy - caught up to a group of six Muslim men. What happened next? If you can just give us a brief chronology of what happened after you met these Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be precise. The group of Muslims was moving towards Konjevic Polje. We did not capture them. We did not take them prisoner. I want to be come completely clear. We caught up with them. They were moving freely without anyone being there. It was not just the case with that particular group. In that period there were already groups that were moving towards Sandici and the other way around, from Sandici to Konjevic Polje, along the route. So we stopped our APC and we took them into the APC. We drove them to Konjevic Polje. There were six of them. And I -- already by that time in Konjevic Polje the crossroads in some torched houses, there were people who were captured who had already surrendered - I'm talking about Muslims - and I, after the APC stopped, told Milo Petrovic that that group of Muslims who were in the APC, he should take them to a group that was in an area of Konjevic Polje. Mile did not reply or say anything to me, he simply led the group away. After that, I went to the other side of the crossroads in front of a house that was in the crossroads area, I sat underneath a balcony, there was a fire burning there, there were five or six men there, Muslims, who had surrendered. After a certain period of time, you could hear a burst of gunfire and then after five, six or ten minutes - I'm speaking approximately - Mile Petrovic appeared. He came up to me and he said, Chief, today, I took revenge for my brother. I looked at him, I said, Mile what have you done? He said, I killed them all. And to be honest, I just looked. I didn't react. I didn't say anything. I didn't even know that his brother was killed or that he did this out of revenge. I didn't comment in any way. I didn't do anything. I simply accepted that as a fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just ask you very simply, do you know a man named Nenad Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Nenad Deronjic is a Bratunac public security station policeman who in that critical period was engaged at the check-point in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Nenad Deronjic at the check-point in Konjevic Polje that day, 13 July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have the same question about a man named Mirko Peric. Did you see him there that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did. He is a member of the same public security station in Bratunac, and he was engaged at the same check-point in the shift that happened to be on duty at the time. And for information purposes only, the check-point in Konjevic Polje was working much earlier before Srebrenica fell. It was a check-point manned by the Bratunac police station, and shifts there were manned by members of that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on a bit now to the afternoon-evening of 13 July 1995, after you returned to Bratunac. And I want to ask you if you were instructed to meet with any senior VRS officers that evening, once you got back to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening, when I came back to Bratunac, after a certain amount of time at the Bratunac Brigade command, I went to dinner or lunch or I don't know what I should call it, I went to the only kitchen that was part of the Bratunac Brigade, and I was informed by the communication centre that I needed to go to the centre of town in Bratunac to meet -- or, actually, Colonel Beara summoned me to meet with him. And as far as I can recall, at about 2000 hours, after I had a little bit to eat, I went -- met with Colonel Beara in the centre of town. I just wand to explain that, so as to avoid misunderstanding, when I say the centre of town, Bratunac is a very small town, it has one main street, one hotel, one municipal building and a few buildings in that part of the town. So wherever you go, you always end up in the centre of town. So I don't want there to be my misunderstanding about that. I got there, I met Colonel Beara, he was standing near a square and I went up to him and said, Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just briefly, for clarity, this is Colonel Beara, the security officer from the Main Staff? Is that who we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And had you met Mr. -- or Colonel Beara before in the course of your duties, without getting into why or how? But was this the first time you met him or had you met him before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not the first time. I know Colonel Beara personally. I knew him. I mean I'm talking about that date. We met several times before this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You said he summonsed you. What happened when you met him? Did he give you any instructions or orders, or what was he calling you to meet with him for?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Beara told me that I need to go to the Zvornik Brigade, that I need to find Drago Nikolic, the security chief of the Zvornik Brigade, and to convey to him personally his order.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last few words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm talking about, well, this is one type of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not all your words were caught by the interpreters. Could you resume from where you said that you needed to find Drago Nikolic, the security chief of the Zvornik Brigade, and to convey to him personally his order. And what did you then say, his order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is more or less everything that I said. I said that I nevertheless considered that to be an order, because this was intelligence-security that was involved. It is understood that the security organs do not issue orders to each other, but this was along the professional line of engagement of the security organ, so I say that as far as I'm concerned, that was still an order that I believed that I should and must carry out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was the content of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The content of the order was that I should go to Zvornik, to the Zvornik Brigade, find Drago Nikolic and convey to him the order that all prisoners that happened to be in Bratunac at that time and who were being brought to Bratunac would be transferred to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade and that Drago Nikolic down there should prepare the area, the people, and receive those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did -- did Colonel Beara tell you what would happen to the prisoners after they arrived in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Beara told me that the Muslim prisoners that were being transferred to Zvornik would be temporarily detained in that area and that after that they would be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what happened next? Did you -- did you obey this order? Did you go to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Zvornik, and I came to the Zvornik Brigade HQ. I reported at the reception. One of the soldiers who was working there assigned a soldier or a military policeman, I don't know which one, I think it was a military policeman, to escort me to a room in the Zvornik Brigade HQ. I was received in that room by an officer. I assume that that was the duty operations room and that was the duty operations officer, and he asked me why I was there. I told him that I was there to convey directly to Drago Nikolic an order from Colonel Beara. After I told him that, he called -- actually he sent a policeman and called one of the officers who came to that same room, and asked me if he could help me in the matter. I said that my order was explicitly to convey the order directly to Drago Nikolic. After that they told me that Drago Nikolic was not at the Zvornik Brigade HQ, that he was at the Forward Command Post and they sent me, since I insisted on seeing Drago Nikolic, then -- I apologise, really. They assigned an officer to escort me and I went to the Forward Command Post. I found Drago Nikolic and I conveyed the order issued to me by Colonel Beara. Other than what I just said, I also told Drago Nikolic what I already knew. We spoke for some five to seven minutes, not longer, and I told Drago that I had information that people who were arriving would be billeted first in Zvornik and then that they would be killed. Drago did not comment. He said that he would report -- report or inform his command about it and then they would see what they would do. After that, I took the same route back with the police officer to the Zvornik Brigade HQ, the policeman stayed there and I continued back to Bratunac to my own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. On the way back to Bratunac from Zvornik, did you see any buses travelling towards Zvornik or did you learn of any buses, become aware of buses travelling towards Zvornik at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my way back to Bratunac, I met or I encountered a few buses going in the direction of Zvornik. After I came to the Bratunac Brigade, I was informed by the military police and the military police commander that the check-point at the Drina bridge by a different road, an old road along the river Drina, in the evening hours some buses left through that check-point, they said there were some five or six buses that left in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you know who were -- who was being transported on those buses, what kind of people?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were transferred who had been captured along the Sandici-Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba-Milici road and who had already been transferred to Bratunac. They were in the buses, they were escorted in the buses, and as such were transferred towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, once you returned to Bratunac, did you make any report to Mr. Beara or did you talk to him again about your -- that you had carried out his order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I returned to Bratunac that night, at about midnight. I went to the Fontana. I found Colonel Beara and reported to him that I had carried out his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what happened? What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, Colonel Beara asked me to take him to the SDS president, Miroslav Deronjic, to his office. And of course, Colonel Beara and I went to the SDS office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who was there? Was Mr. Deronjic there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Colonel Beara and I came to the SDS office, Colonel Beara was there as well as Colonel Dragomir Vasic, the chief of the Zvornik centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what happened? If you could just tell us what you remember happening next?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, they had an argument at the very beginning, Colonel Beara and Miroslav Deronjic. They were both shouting. Miroslav Deronjic requested that all prisoners leave Bratunac, and I'm going to say something here which I know is absurd but I want to tell the Trial Chamber exactly what happened. At that point in time, since there was general chaos, a situation that could not be controlled absolutely, it was beyond any control, if we are talking about the situation in Bratunac, there was a lot of buses, there were a lot of trucks in Bratunac, there was no street in Bratunac without buses, trucks and captured Muslims. The reason why I went to Zvornik when Colonel Beara told me to go there was that those Muslims would be transferred to Zvornik. Then at that meeting, he insisted that the Muslims remain in Bratunac. So then things were not clear to me either. Deronjic was very strongly opposed to that, and he said to him that he did not want the Muslims to be in Bratunac and that he did not want the killing to be carried out in Bratunac. For the Trial Chamber I would like to state this here. Then on the 20th -- no, actually, on the 13th in the evening at 12.00 midnight - actually it was already the 14th because it was after midnight - there was absolutely no further question regarding the fate of those Muslims. It was known that they would be killed. The question and the discussion was solely about whether they would be killed in Bratunac or transferred to Zvornik and killed there. And this is what I heard and saw with my own ears and eyes. So both of them in that argument cited instructions that they had received from their chiefs. Miroslav Deronjic directly said, I received an order from President Karadzic that they should all go to Zvornik. Beara said, I received an order from my boss that they should stay here in Bratunac. And that was the argument, the quarrel, between the two of them about who received what sort of instruction from their bosses. Of course, I don't know what instructions they received but I'm just telling you what I heard and what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you speak at this meeting? Did you take part yourself?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not take part in the argument about the status of the prisoners, and so on and so forth. As far as I can remember, Colonel Vasic also did not take part in the discussion. This was an argument between Deronjic and Beara. When they finished with that part, then at that same meeting they discussed -- they talked normally. Once the argument was over, Miroslav Deronjic sat down. They took out little glasses and he poured himself and Beara something. They drank that. I don't know what it was but they drank it. And then after that they discussed what needed to be done that night in order to secure Bratunac because it was in absolute chaos. It was ordered to engage the civilian police, the military police, and also to use loudspeakers during the night so that the Bratunac Brigade military police and the Bratunac civilian police in a military vehicle with a loudspeaker drove around the inner area of Bratunac calling on all those armed and civilians who had weapons to come out and to provide those who had come to Bratunac that night, they were arriving from Kasaba, there was a large number of buses from Konjevic Polje, trucks, a large number of prisoners, so it was really general chaos. Chaos prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, do we go to 10.35 or break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's 10.28. We will have a break in two minutes, but if you think that you should not start a new subject then we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we have two minutes, I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you said earlier they referred to their chiefs. Who was -- in your understanding, who was Mr. Beara referring to when he spoke about his boss's instructions that the prisoners should remain in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that all of us officers, including myself, I also referred to General Mladic as chief or the boss. Everybody did that. And as far as us officers, he was the only boss, the only chief. So I think that there is no dilemma that he was thinking of General Mladic, that is how we all referred to him, including Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break, but could first the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you on schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe I am, Your Honour. I think I can make my time or if I do not, I will be begging for just a little bit more, not too much more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to stay within your own time estimates. We will take a break and we will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, while that is being done Ms. Lindsay asked me to inform the Chamber that if at all possible she would like to return to the United States on Thursday some time. There is a medical hearing tomorrow. Could I ask that the Chamber keep that in mind when it schedules the amount of time for the medical hearing tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course we are not fully in control, Ms. Lindsay, by the way I should have put on the record that you were presents again as you were last week, Thursday, I think it was. We will keep it in mind, but as you will also understand that we are not in full control. At the same time I think that matters until now have not caused great concerns. So at least I have not heard of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if you're ready you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Nikolic, just moving along, I'm going to ask you some questions now about the 14th of July, 1995. We just discussed the meeting. What happened to the prisoners, the Muslim men, who were being had held in Bratunac on the 14th of July 1995? Did they stay in Bratunac or were they transported somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the prisoners who were in Bratunac on 14 July, either at the detention facilities or on buses and trucks, were moved as part of a convoy in the morning of -- on the 14th, to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you know, could you tell us which units or bodies served as escorts for the convoy of prisoners to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope I can be very precise when you ask -- in answering this. Those structures that provided security in some of the facilities, and they were predominantly the police, either civilian or military, so the same structures that provided security for these facilities, they also escorted the convoy. The escorts of the buses and trucks where the prisoners, Muslim prisoners had been kept overnight, the escorts that were on the buses and the trucks, they also provided security for the convoy. So I also have to tell you that as part of the security of this transport, there were various units of the civilian police, the security station in Bratunac, members of the special brigade of the MUP of Republika Srpska even, and finally, when all other resources had been used, there were also civilians who participated in escorting these buses and trucks. They were armed and they went as escorts of these buses or trucks in civilian clothes. And they assisted either the military or the civilian police as part of the security detail of these convoys. So most generally speaking, these were the kind of people who participated in providing security of the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have D00285, English page 14, Serbian page 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, while this is coming up this is the Bratunac Brigade military police daily log and I want to show you one entry. So we can see an entry now that says, "Daily report 14/15 July 1995," and it says, "The police was engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees." Can you just tell us, if you know, what this military police log entry refers to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this is a daily logbook of the military police, and in those daily reports usually you would note the daily employment of members of the military police platoon of the brigade, and then of course here I see that they were engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees, the date is the 14th, and this cannot be a reference to anything else because on that day, whoever was available was engaged on this particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you say anything else, and on that date, just to be clear, is that the transport of the prisoners in the convoy to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring exclusively and only to those men, because there was no other transport other than this convoy, at least I can't recall that there was any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on now a little bit to another topic, and that is -- concerns the local staff, in other words Muslim employees of humanitarian organisations and international organisations in the enclave. And I'd like to show you 65 ter 04242. While it's coming up I'll just read that this is from the Bratunac Brigade intel organs. The date is 18 July 1995. And it's got your name at the bottom. Do you remember this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what I want to focus on - your copy is a bit blurry - the last portion, which states: "Will you please tell me what stand to take in terms of authorisation for evacuation of the international organisation Medecins Sans Frontieres? In fact, how to deal with so-called local staff. This also applies to the interpreters of military monitors and UNPROFOR. RDB," which CLSS says -- said is regional state security, "passed on to us an opinion that President Karadzic had allegedly abolished all local staff who used to work for UNPROFOR. It is our opinion that they should not be hold -- or held." So can you just tell us briefly what's going on here? What does this paragraph refer to about the president saying -- conveying that local staff should be "abolished," as it says in our version?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope it is clear what we -- what is meant by local staff. As for this, simply put, in my language, abolition means, in fact, freeing or releasing someone from responsibility, and if I understand this properly, if that is what he meant, that they should be considered free of any responsibility, there was no need to release them or anything similar because all the local staff, the employees who worked at these international organisations, including UNPROFOR, the military monitors, and other international organisations that were in Srebrenica, who had Muslim local staff, these people had not committed anything that would have been considered a crime that would then call for an abolition. So it is -- it was our opinion, and you can see there in the last paragraph, that they should not be held. That was my position and the position of the officer who was in my office, Colonel Jankovic, and we considered that all those who were employed and who worked there should leave, together with their employers, on the convoys that were leaving Potocari, in other words to leave the enclave and go wherever they chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I see the next page of the Serbian or B/C/S, please? Sorry, and then the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, there is also a handwritten version of this document. Can you tell us whose handwriting that is, if you know, and why there is a handwritten version and also a typed version, if you can explain that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see this document before me. This is not my handwriting. In other words, I did not author this. And this is an illustration of the situation which I mentioned on the first day of my evidence here. During this critical period, in other words throughout the activities in the area of responsibility of my brigade, Colonel Radislav Jankovic from the Main Staff was assigned to my office, and just in order to clarify why he was the one who wrote these things, whereas in the typewritten form there is my signature as the author of the document, the reason for this is the following: This was the regular procedure when reports were sent to superior commands; in other words, the report is written out by hand, then it is taken to the communication centre where this handwritten text would be typed and sent off, and the operative who had typed it up would return it to the original source, in other words to me, both the original handwritten text and the typewritten text. So both Colonel Jankovic and I had drafted this report. I had -- I took it to the communication centre to be retyped and sent, and of course the operative -- the operations officer there - he knew me because we were in daily contact - he typed it up and then sent it to me for signature. So we can see from the original that this was written by Colonel Jankovic and me, but in the typewritten text we see that the duty operations officer when retyping it, when typing it up, he put my name down and brought it to me for signature. But the content and everything is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we just go to the next page in the Serbian, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know what that little R or the little sort of initials are on the bottom left, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is just what I was telling you about. You can see that Radislav Jankovic initialled this. He was the officer from the Main Staff that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04242 receives number P1515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm almost at the end, Mr. Nikolic. What I want to ask you about now is what you can tell us about any operation to rebury the bodies of Muslim men who had been executed after the fall of Srebrenica, and I'm specifically talking about men who had been buried in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a lot about this issue. The only question is what it is that you want to hear. What is it that you would like me to answer? I know everything, how it transpired from the very beginning through the end of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, let me ask you first when you learned about this operation and who you learned it -- whom you learned it from, who gave the order for this operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in September, Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic came to the command of my Bratunac Brigade. He was the chief of security in the Drina Corps. And he conveyed to my commander, and then to me, an order to the effect that there was a decision by the Main Staff that the graves from Glogova should be moved to the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you know the people, the bodies in the graves in Glogova, where were they -- when had they been buried there, the ones that were to be moved?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is this: All those people who were killed in Kravica and all the people who were killed on those critical days on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road and in the area of the Bratunac and Srebrenica municipalities were transported and buried in two mass graves near Glogova, in a village near -- within the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests that the witness repeat the names because it's not certain that they are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said "... in a village near...," and what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Glogova village which belongs to the Bratunac municipality; in other words, it is on the territory of the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I read literally from the transcript and see whether we have now everything. You said that those who were killed "were transported and buried in two mass graves near Glogova, in a village near --" and did you then again want to say Glogova, or did you in second instance mention another name where you continued by saying within the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that they were buried and I believe I'm not getting the right interpretation, so they were buried in Glogova village, not near Glogova. They were buried in Glogova in two mass graves, and then I said that Glogova village was in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked for a little bit more. We are now at 20 minutes. Could you please try to wind up as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I have another -- if I'm not wrong, I have until quarter until, unless I'm wrong. I thought I had 45 minutes this session to be within my time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I made a mistake. Apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. I see that I was thinking of 75 minutes whereas it is 105 minutes. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now then can you just -- and this is a compound question, but I think you can deal with it. Can you tell us if this operation to relocate the bodies was carried out, and if it was, which organs, units or personnel, carried it out? In other words, did it happen, and if these bodies were moved, who took part in that process?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The operation was carried out. And I will try now to mention all the names of the ones who participated in the operation. The initiative came from the civilian authorities, and after this initiative, Popovic told us that the decision had been taken to move the bodies from those two graves in Glogova to the Srebrenica municipality territory. In this operation, the Bratunac Brigade participated, specifically the military police which provided security on the road, and redirected the traffic during the operation itself to other routes. The same task was assigned to the civilian police from Bratunac, in other words the public security station there. Then in addition to these units, the civilian and the military police, the 5th Engineering Battalion participated in this operation as well which is part of the Drina Corps. In the planning and organisation of this entire operation, there were also -- and in providing and securing the equipment, the earth-moving machines, there were the executive authorities of the Bratunac municipality, the president of the municipality, of the assembly, and the chairman of the SDS. The president of the Executive Council's task was to provide logistical support from those companies that had construction machines, the ULTs, the diggers and other machines that were used in this operation. The companies that participated in this were the utilities company, the public utilities company in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the next company name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the companies from the Srebrenica municipality, in other words the Sase mine and their machines, the transport company from Srebrenica and their trucks, and the construction company Radnik and their construction -- their earth moving machines. I believe these were the ULT or U-L-T machines. I think I haven't omitted anyone. These were the participants in this operation of the movement, transfer and reburial of the bodies from the Glogova graves to Srebrenica. I have to say that at the very outset this operation was supposed to be a covert operation and there were attempts to organise it as such. However, in view of the number of parties that took part in this operation, and the length of the operation itself, I believe it took about two months, with gaps in between. There were many parties that took part in it, many people who took part, so that a few days later, it was no longer covert. Everyone knew what it was all about. I believe it's also important to mention that we received the fuel for this operation, in other words the Bratunac Brigade received the fuel from the Drina Corps command from their logistical service, and on two occasions, the first time five tonnes and the second time two tonnes of fuel, I believe, and it was ordered that the expenditure of the fuel should be monitored by the organs and provide reports on how it had been dealt with for this entire operation. We proceeded according to the order, and as a security organ I briefed my commander on a daily basis either orally or when we met, but certainly during the regular daily briefing meetings. This would be in brief about this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Could I have 65 ter 04204A, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to tell us the second company you mentioned, because the interpreters didn't catch everything because of the high speed of your telling us, you said the companies that participated in this were the public utilities company in Bratunac. And the interpreters didn't get the next name. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, of course. It's the Rad [phoen] Bratunac utility company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just from the cover page, Mr. Nikolic, do you recognise this document which we have, reports of meetings of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade in our translation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I go to page 2 of this excerpt, please? Now, this is dated 16 October 1995. It's headed, "Working meeting of commander and command staff and battalion commanders." I just want to focus on the part on the bottom which is by your name, and, in fact, on the last point: "We are currently engaged in tasks issued by the Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff (hygiene and sanitation measures.)" And it says in the Serbian "asanacija" in those parentheses. Can you just tell us what this -- well, if you remember making this contribution to the meeting and what it was about? What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are minutes from the meeting at the Bratunac Brigade command, Nikolic in the minutes is me, and the sentence that you read is what I was talking about before. I informed the commander that we were working on duties from the VRS Main Staff. My operation was being conducted under the name "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, so just to be very clear, when you say what I was talking about before, is that the reburial operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the operation that I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last few words the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last few words of his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe I should just ask the question again, Your Honour, would that be simpler?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not clear to me on the basis of the transcript that there was anything following, but apparently there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't see it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again, Mr. Nikolic, sorry. When you said -- the operation you were talking about before, does this entry for the meeting on 16 October 1995 we just discussed at the bottom, "asanacija," does that refer to the reburial operation we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does refer to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04204A receives number P1516, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we decide on admission, Mr. Nicholls, the cover page says reports, meetings. Is this an extract from a larger set of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours. I understood that the procedure was to make an extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have one small other question. There is some handwriting on the cover page in the original which is not translated. Now, it seems to me that it's a note about where the document has been found and when it has been found. If that is what it is, and if the Defence does not object, then we could leave it like that. Is that what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To be honest, I hadn't noticed, Your Honour. Thank you. I think you're correct, that does look like a post-it, actually, to me that got photocopied on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, any problems to have it admitted without this specific part which is not a part of the original document being translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence does not have any problems.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes: We did not hear what the Defence counsel said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not everything was heard by the interpreters, Mr. Petrusic. You said the Defence does not have any problems and it to be admitted in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P1516 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you to my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, that's basically all the questions I have at this time about these events. I would like to ask you how you feel about having participated in these events and if there is anything you would like to say.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I use the opportunity every time, and I would like to do it this time as well, to apologise to all the victims. I would like to apologise to all the families who survived this horrendous crime. I would like to say that I'm very sorry and that I feel terrible, and I would like to say that I made a mistake that when I became aware that crimes would take place, that I did not pick up and run away and leave, because I did assist individually in this operation. I did help certain Muslims, some families, and they survived, thank God, but I think that that was not enough, and I'm very sorry that in carrying out my orders I participated in the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. I have one additional question for you. This whole reburial operation could you tell us, do you know, what the thoughts behind it were? Why was it done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know for sure is that that's the only reason this was done, because allegedly it was done to conceal the crime and to distribute this all over the area belonging to Srebrenica, thus the main objective in my opinion is concealment of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I have to understand it in such a way that bringing the bodies closer to where combat may have taken place, that it would be easier to explain that there were combat casualties which might be more difficult to explain if the bodies were found at a larger distance from where combat activities may have taken place during the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honours, that the places where the remains were buried and transferred from the Glogova area, the position has no major significance because the places where they were buried, there were no positions there, nor was fighting conducted there. In view of a large number of these secondary graves that were dug in the Srebrenica area, with the bodies being transferred there, I think that the transfer, now, you could not justify anything with it or bring into doubt the fact that a crime was carried out. From what I understand, it would not be possible to use that to justify it or to look for an excuse, and that in this way there was a desire to present those victims as victims of military combat. This is the first thing that occurs to me now, but I think the main reason is that the transfer and concealment of the crime is the reason because a large number of those killed were buried in these graves. I don't know if this assists you in any way but this is what occurs to me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one other question for you. I read part of one of your answers and it's about the local Muslim staff. You said: "These people had not committed anything that would have been considered a crime that would then call for an abolition." I do understand that we are talking about local staff being employed by the international organisations. What was the -- I see you're nodding yes. If you say that would then call for an abolition, I mean what would anyone have to do with relieving from their duties apart from those international organisations themselves? What had the people meeting to do with whether they would be relieved from their duties in the context of their employment? That's what I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I have the correct interpretation, I think -- well, I will try very briefly to clarify things. It's like this: This was local staff, these were people, Muslims, from Srebrenica who spent all of their time working for the needs of international organisations, including DutchBat, and when all the Muslims, all the civilians, all those who came to Potocari, when they were transferred or were separated, so when there was nobody in Potocari any more except for DutchBat members and international organisations that stayed and that were waiting to leave last, there were Muslims among them who were members or, rather, citizens of the Srebrenica municipality who worked for them, and of course, as people who had nothing to do with combat activities, were not members of war units, and that there was no suspicion that they had done anything except for the fact that they were employed by the international organisations who were there, this is what I was thinking of. There was no need for any of them to be pardoned because they didn't do anything. They were working, they were not soldiers, they did not commit any crimes and, as such, now they were supposed to leave the enclave together with the employees that they were working for. Had it not been like that, had there been a decision for them to keep them, to separate them, from their employers, then they would have ended up in the same position as those who had been transferred to the school, Vuk Karadzic, transferred to Zvornik and subsequently killed. So to me, that is the main point. They stayed there, they remained, because they were employed at their employers and they left in a convoy together with them, and then after that according to the information that I have they went to different countries where they wanted to go. But I assert, in any event, that there was no need for any kind of amnesty or pardon because they didn't do anything. And this is how I understand that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now do you know whether that happened, you referred to them leaving and ending up in different countries, did all the local staff -- was treated in such a way that they were free to go and/or were some or some of them also treated like the other able-bodied men who were often taken, brought to various places? Do you know whether they, the local staff, was in that respect privileged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, I know of only one case of Mr. Nuhanovic and his family, that participated in negotiations at the Fontana Hotel. And later, in view of the fact that I know his son and that I know the entire situation, later they did not want to keep Nuhanovic and protect him. He left in a convoy or was separated, I really don't know precisely what happened, but according to information that I had, based on what Colonel Jankovic told me, because he was in charge of all of these contacts and decisions, I know that all of those who happened to be there on the last day when DutchBat was leaving the Srebrenica enclave or Potocari, they went together in that convoy with the DutchBat, as part of that convoy. This is what I know and this is what Colonel Jankovic conveyed to me after the last soldier left Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say the position of Mr. Nuhanovic was exceptional compared to other local staff employed by the international organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not his situation but that of his brother and his father, because he was an interpreter, he asked for his father and his brother, I'm not sure who exactly, that they be protected and that they stay there. But this was not permitted, according to the information that I have, so I don't know how they ended up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I intended to refer to his family members but thank you for those answers. Mr. Petrusic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question for the witness, so if you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, when Mr. Prosecutor asked you about questions about local staff you talked about Karadzic having said they must be abolished, and Judge Orie asks to you clarify this point you are talking about, they did nothing that needed a pardon. I'm not quite sure I understand what the meaning of abolition means in the answer that you gave previously. Are you able to tell us what abolition meant in that context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I personally didn't mean anything. I was just interpreting what was written in the report. Information came from the RDB, the State Security Service, that allegedly Karadzic "abolirati," pardoned the local population. I was just interpreting what this means, "abolicija." What does it mean to amnesty or pardon someone? The person subject to the abolition, and I'm speaking about practice in my country, means that you had to have committed some criminal act in order to be pardoned. Simply speaking in my language, for somebody to forgive you for that crime. But what I meant was that there was nothing to forgive because they didn't do anything wrong. This is what I was explaining, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This really clarifies the word used, I think, a lot for the Judges. Mr. Petrusic, if you're ready you can start your cross-examining. Mr. Nikolic you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Petrusic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- yes. Cross-examination Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, at the very beginning I want to tell you something that you know, and that is that we need to pause between question and answer so that we could receive a complete interpretation. And I would also like you to slow down your natural rhythm of speech, your pace. In your CV you said that you completed the faculty of All People's Defence. I would like to ask you this: That faculty of All People's Defence, was that something that was in line with the generally accepted concept of All People's Defence that was in force in our society, in the society of former Yugoslavia, and the former JNA as well, the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that faculty gave you certain military knowledge which later you conveyed when you were teaching to younger generations in the subjects that you were teaching in high school?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I worked in the high school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You spent seven or eight years working as assistant TO commander of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was assistant commander from 1986 until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you were carrying out those posts, did you acquire some practical experience in terms of military exercises, courses, continual -- continuous education and training in those topics?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did complete a certain number of courses, and I took part in the command staff exercises as part of the TO staff in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that period, from the late 80s, the exercises you could say were frequent?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about different things. The exercises were not that frequent but the training was frequent, the actual exercises are something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I didn't use the correct terms. But in any case, the training courses which you attended were they courses that had to do exclusively with the area of intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part they were on intelligence and security matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The concept that was in force at the time, and the position that you had as assistant commander of the TO, did that train you so that in the event of war you could command certain military units of the Territorial Defence, which again, according to that concept, comprised all those who were not part of the JNA active forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not quite understand you but I will try to answer. Well, you can also go and complete your education in a military academy for a certain military specialty and then as an officer you are trained for a certain military occupational specialty. And I'm an infantry man, so after completing that education I was assigned to the TO staff where I held a position which meant that I was at the rank of an officer and given the rank of an officer immediately. Training for command and control is something that goes on gradually. You are not trained to command and control immediately after you finish school. You are given duties in that sense and then later you are guided through those posts and functions through exercises, training, and that is how you acquire your capability for that particular duty. I hope that that is what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you were given the rank of officer, is that when you were actually given the rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was done gradually. First of all I was 2nd lieutenant, lieutenant, and then captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The armed conflict or clashes in the April-May period in the territory of Bratunac municipality, what was your practical role as assistant commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is very complex in terms of the period to which you are referring. I could be very precise in my answer had the entire staff not fallen apart. Now, you know the way that these staffs were established. In my staff, in other words, where I was assigned, the Staff Commander was a Muslim; the assistant commander for operations and training and at the same time a deputy commander of the TO was a Muslim. And in that structure, and I won't go into every detail, all of these people in Bratunac in 1992 left the staff and fled from Bratunac. And the only people remaining in the staff were me, Milisav Stojanovic, Rajko Banjac and Mirko -- I can't remember the last name. So this was something that wasn't really a staff anymore and could not operate as a whole. So my role in the staff, in the period that you were referring to, was to make an effort to establish a new staff, to establish and man units because Territorial Defence units had been manned and established in the same manner, at least 50 per cent would have been Muslims. That's before the war. And now I had to deal with this, establishing staffs and units, staffs, commands and units of the Territorial Defence according to the establishment as it was prescribed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you at any point become a member of the Crisis Staff of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear which municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my function as the acting Staff Commander, I was a member of the Crisis Staff of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I'm looking at the clock, if this would be a suitable time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree but I kind of lost -- I'm not sure when the break should be. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think now. And then perhaps we hear an answer after the break to your question who was the commander, unless the witness could tell us in one word who the commander was, the commander of the Crisis Staff? Is that -- witness, could you tell us who the commander of the Crisis Staff was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the president of the municipality, by -- in the -- because of his function as the president of the municipality, would have been the commander of the staff, either him or the president of the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could then the witness be escorted out of the courtroom? We will take a break and we would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 12.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile I use the time for the following matter: On the 8th of May this year the Prosecution has sent a memorandum to the Chamber and to the Defence proposing to hold short procedural discussions or Rule 65 ter meetings, and the purpose would be to identify proposed Prosecution experts relevant to the Srebrenica segment of the case for whom the Defence does not have new areas of inquiry other than those already challenged in previous cases. Now, the Chamber also understands that subsequently, that the parties are actively discussing this issue among themselves and the Chamber will await the outcome of those discussions and will not become involved in these discussions at this stage. I am looking to Prosecution/Defence. I see a slight nodding yes on both parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution also considered the Chamber's ruling with respect to expert witnesses last week as also being dispositive of this and making this question moot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Petrusic, if you're ready you may continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
