utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, apologies for being impolite and continuing our discussions when you entered the courtroom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before I resume with questions, Mr. Nikolic, to my last question, you replied that the president of the Crisis Staff was either the president of the municipality or the chairman of the SDS. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This was for the purposes of the transcript because the transcript reflected that it was either the president of the municipality or the president of the Executive Board -- Executive Committee. Now, the president of the municipality was Miroslav Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did he have a lot of power within the civilian structures at that time, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you take into account that he was the president of the municipal board of the SDS and that after the first multi-party elections, it was the time after the first multi-party elections, of course everyone of any relevance in Bratunac was in the civilian structures and in the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Deronjic retain his powers until 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe until he was arrested, that was the case. Nothing of any significance really changed from the first multi-party elections up until his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was sometime in 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't remember the exact date but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, between May and November, you were not within the structures of the Territorial Defence and from what I could see in all the documents, I can't see that you were anywhere in Bratunac either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which year, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, for a while, in the period between May up until about October or November, I was not a member -- anywhere on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this was your personal decision, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not my personal decision. There was -- I was assaulted physically and after that I had to be hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were the persons who assaulted you, were they indicted?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of those people who had assaulted me were killed. They got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After November 1992 did you ever have similar problems? I mean, were you assaulted?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I tried to do my job properly, there were all kinds of conflicts with various structures, beginning with volunteers and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you returned to Bratunac in 1992, you returned to the Bratunac Brigade -- you went to the Bratunac Brigade. What was your rank at the time, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I had the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were -- the then commander proposed that you be appointed to this post. Who was it who appointed you to that duty?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed in late 1992 after my return from Belgrade to the duty of chief of the security and intelligence organ in the Bratunac Brigade. I was appointed pursuant to the proposal by the then-commander in Bratunac, and the appointment itself under the law was carried out by the administration or the sector or the department of security and intelligence and all the personnel issues were ordered and any other measures were ordered by the commander of the Main Staff, and I believe that was how it was under the then-legal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you were -- you could not be appointed to the chief of -- to the post of chief of security and intelligence unless that proposal came from a superior command, which would in this case be at least the Drina Corps command; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- my commander and the immediate superior command were -- would give their own opinions on who it was to be appointed and I suppose that no one in this security and intelligence administration within the Main Staff would have appointed me if the opinions from those other sources were negative on me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last part of the answer? You said "... if the opinions from those other sources were negative on me." That's the last what is recorded. Did you add anything after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said if the opinion from my command or from the immediate superior command, which was the Drina Corps command, were to be negative, then I'm absolutely certain that I would not have been appointed to that duty by the organ in the Main Staff that was charged -- that dealt with appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me conclude this with one final question. Once you were appointed, your commander and all your superior commands had sufficient information about your professionalism and your competence and they were certain that you could carry out properly the duties in the Bratunac Brigade of chief of security and intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just have to correct you for the purpose of the transcript, to be precise. I was not the chief of the administration. I was the chief of the organ for security and intelligence in the brigade. The administration was in the Main Staff only. Now, as to what my colleagues thought about me and my competence, I really don't know. You'd have to ask them. But I do consider that I was sufficiently trained in order to be able to carry out those duties properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, it's only now that the translation ends. But the last three pages of transcript, the Chamber is fully unaware of what the relevance of questions and answers could be and I'm not seeking an explanation, but we would rather hear questions for which it is immediately clear what the relevance is. So would you please keep in mind that we like to hear relevant evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, were there any criminal proceedings initiated against you in Bratunac before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no criminal proceedings against me in Bratunac before the conflict broke out. I was accused of having purchased 500 Swiss franks from a person who had returned from Switzerland where he had worked. Now, since you're asking this I can tell you why this criminal report was submitted at all. It was submitted because at the time I was supposed to be appointed the police commander for regional traffic. In order to eliminate me from this post, so I wouldn't even be a candidate, this charge was brought against me falsely because it wasn't even based on a criminal offence. This would have been an offence against the dealing in foreign currency, according to the then-laws. Now, once this criminal report was submitted, it never really got anywhere. I never -- I was never even brought before a court. It was never taken to trial. It was quashed. So the only purpose of this criminal report was to eliminate me as a possible candidate. Never in my life had I been indicted or accused of anything or charged with any charges, neither now or ever before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we now please see 65 ter 1D01028? Mr. Nikolic, this is information provided by the commander of the police station in Bratunac, which reads, in the second paragraph -- or states, rather, that you are filed in operative criminal records due to the commission of the criminal offence from Article 167, paragraph 1, of the criminal code of the SFRY dating from the 20th of February, 1987, jointly with some other persons. And what is characteristic in this report is that there is no copy of this criminal report because it had disappeared at an unidentified points in time and under unclear circumstances. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We didn't receive any interpretation. Could you please repeat your question, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, this information that was read out to you is slightly different from the answer that you gave us earlier because the information states that the criminal report was indeed filed but that it disappeared. So the criminal proceedings under the then-laws of the SFRY were instigated against you, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question was whether criminal proceedings were held against you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I remember exactly what this was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, please don't interrupt me. Please don't interrupt me. Don't interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't both talk at the same time. Please put clear -- yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just -- I have an objection, Your Honour, to the mischaracterisation of his testimony and answer earlier. My friend just said that this is different because it states that the criminal court was indeed filed. What Mr. Nikolic says at page 50, line 1: "Now, since you're asking this, I can tell you why this criminal report was submitted at all." So he did say that there was something submitted in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Mr. Petrusic, you have dealt with the matter but I could ask the witness as well. Mr. Nikolic, Article 167 of the criminal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia deals with what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the law then in force in 1984 the code, legal criminal code, Article 167 refers to the criminal act of trade in gold coins and foreign currency. And it was considered a crime, the article had two paragraphs, the first was milder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. It is apparently the same kind of offence. Now, Mr. Nikolic said that the case was never brought to court, never -- I see here that it says, "The above mentioned person is filed in an operative criminal record." It doesn't say anything about any follow-up. We could ask the witness whether he has any knowledge of this, how this disappeared, whether he know that is it disappeared and whether he knows the circumstances. Could you tell us, Mr. Nikolic, but would could you please focus your answers very much on the questions put to you? For example, the last question you told us why had happened. That was not the question. So do you know anything about the disappearance of this file?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I never worked at the MUP. I never entered there. And I don't know anything, absolutely, about the disappearance of the criminal report from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the question. You have now answered. Any follow-up questions, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on this matter, Your Honour, no. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1028 receives number D297, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, is it in the description of your duties of the intelligence security organ, and were you able to, in the course of your work, interrogate prisoners of war, carry out their security processing, as it's referred to, and similar duties?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you the one who was authorised to identify a certain person as being of interest for security processing or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any person, any person that would come from the other side, from the other side meaning the territory on the other side, either as an escapee or a prisoner of war, was of security interest and we took the statement and interviewed each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple answer would therefore be "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, very well, Your Honour. I will try to -- I will do my best to respect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you know in July 1995 that there was a list at the Bratunac Brigade of persons who were described as persons who committed certain crimes, considered war crimes, and these were people of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to be precise. I knew that in my section, my organ, there was a list of persons for whom there were indications that they had committed crimes and other criminal acts against the civilian population and Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us how many people were on that list?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the exact number because I don't remember any more, but the final list, I think I gave to the institute in Belgrade to a person called Mr. Ivanisevic. I think he's the person who has the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the list of the 12th of July that was made at the Bratunac Brigade command, or, rather, to be precise, do you know of a list of war criminals known to the command of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade drafted in Bratunac on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see that list, I saw that document, but I assert that it did not originate from my organ and I did not draft the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate who would have been able to make that list?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another person who dealt with these matters, to a greater degree than I did, regarding the questioning and documenting of war criminals, is Zlatan Celanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did Zlatan inform you about the things that he was doing as part of his work?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Zlatan does not need to tell me about his work. I knew exactly what Slavko Celanovic was doing and what the commander had ordered him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So if Zlatan Celanovic was more involved in the drafting of this list, would you agree with me, then, that you also were aware of it, you knew about it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you, when you put questions, if you want to quote what I said, then to quote what I actually said and not to just try to plant things. So I -- I did not say that Zlatko Celanovic for the most part took part in the drafting of that list. I did not say that. I said that the only person who could have and who was also dealing with those matters other than myself in the brigade is Zlatan Celanovic but I did not at any point say that he actually drafted that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you sent reports to your superior command, did you send that to the Drina Corps or did you send that to the security organ of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always sent my reports to the intelligence security section of the Drina Corps. That would be the reporting along the professional line. I never addressed my dispatches or reports to the commander except in exceptional circumstances at the request of the commander. I would always send the documents to the intelligence security department of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So those reports went along that line?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was the procedure the same when the Drina Corps sent you reports, to the intelligence security department?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The superior command does not send reports to the subordinate command. The superior command sends information and orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If Popovic sent any report to you, as the Drina Corps security organ, would that report be addressed to your organ, namely the intelligence security organ of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Popovic were to send anything that had to do only with the intelligence security organ of the Bratunac Brigade, and if this were to be addressed to the department for intelligence and security, then that dispatch or information or order or instruction would come to my desk. And just one more thing: That document and any other document for the brigade would previously go to the desk of the brigade commander and then he, through the office, the records office, he would indicate to whom that particular document would need to be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I have a problem with your question. At page 55 line 21, to lines 22, the witness says: "The superior command does not send reports to the subordinate command. The superior command sends information and orders." And the next question you ask is: "If Popovic sent any report to you as the Drina Corps security organ, would that report be addressed to your organ, namely the intelligence security organ of the Bratunac Brigade?" Exactly what he says doesn't happen. Of course, his answer to that question, counsel, refers to information and instructions but your question -- you're asking exactly what he says never happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I used the wrong term, Your Honour, meaning "report," and I can rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were dispatches, telegrams, that were -- or any other acts sent from the Drina Corps, from the security organ to the security organ of the Bratunac Brigade, go directly to the desk of Mr. Nikolic? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this question was already answered by the witness, page 56, line 1 through 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did the Drina Corps have a liaison officer with international organisations, either humanitarian ones or any other kind of international organisation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The word liaison officer, Drina Corps liaison officer with international organisation, any dispute about ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything, though most of our liaison officers are at the brigade level that I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrusic, when you said, "Did the Drina Corps have a liaison officer," did you mean at the corps level or at any lower level to be included?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I meant the Drina Corps command, at the corps level, not at the level of the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then now the question is at least clear to me. Please proceed. Liaison officer with the international organisation at the corps level of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already answered that question. What I know, even though this is not a question for me, is that I had information that there was such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was that Vukota Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Vukota Vukovic was an officer, a signals officer, at the Pribicevac IKM but he did only tasks relating to the Skelani Battalion and the area of responsibility relating to the 3rd Infantry Battalion of my brigade and the Skelani Battalion, but he did not cover the entire AOR of my brigade and of course the Milici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not receive interpretation at this moment. Could you restart your question, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, when you were carrying out your duties as liaison officer, was there any need for you to have contacts and co-operation with the liaison officer of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you put the first question to me, I meant the liaison officer of the Drina Corps who was based at the Drina Corps. This is how I understood it. And then after -- this is how I understood it after the intervention of His Honour. But now I see what you're asking me. You're asking me about Vukota Vukovic. He was appointed by General Zivanovic on behalf of the Drina Corps to have contacts and be a liaison officer at that place where he was and that was Pribicevac where my 3rd Infantry Battalion was and the Skelani Independent Battalion. Only for that area, that officer, liaison officer, of the Drina Corps, Colonel Vukovic, did have contacts with international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P1505, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an information prepared by Slavko Ognjenovic dated the 4th of July, 1994, and let's please see the next page, the paragraph that was quoted earlier in the session on the 30th of May. Now, Mr. Nikolic, if I understood you correctly, according to what you said on page 1178, in this paragraph beginning with -- beginning just above paragraph 3 on page 2, you said there, you expressed your opinion in the following manner: "The enemy -- the life of the enemy should be made impossible and it should be made impossible for them to remain in the enclave, so they should be made to leave en masse the enclave as soon as possible realising that there was no survival for them there."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The page in the English was moved from where it should have been previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, according to what you said on page 1178, what is that a reference to, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a reference to Mr. Nikolic's answer to this question, and because it wasn't clear to me I just wanted to clarify it now by citing that portion of the text in this information that was drafted by Slavko Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nikolic, what I have read out to you is this what you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could just have the cite because there is no page 1178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That was my question, Mr. Petrusic. What -- page of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I -- I can quote again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I want to know -- Mr. Petrusic, I want to know page 1178 of what, of the phone book or of Dostoyevsky or from a testimony given in another case?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, the transcript of -- that's the page of the transcript on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which transcript? In another case?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1178, okay, let's see what I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The transcript of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1178 is a page which covers the testimony of Mr. Kingory and Witness RM255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In my view -- my view, the 30th of May, 2013, the transcript starts with page 11766.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently your thinking in terms of a range of pages somewhere in the 11.000s, where what you said was 1178 is -- or did you mean 11078? Let me just look at where we are. 30th of May starts with 11766 indeed. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page that we quoted was 11788.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 88. Now the matter has been clarified. 11788. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Since we are in the process of correcting dates and numbers, the document on the screen is not from the 14th of July, 1995, but the 4th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you now repeat your question and we have page 11788, at least I have it before me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honours. It's 1994, the document, not 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are correct. You're correct. That was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't there a play which is called the Comedy of Errors where perhaps it comes closes to a tragedy of errors? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in this information it says that the enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they would leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, in an organised manner, realising that they cannot survive there. For you, is this sentence unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that that sentence was unacceptable to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The sentence which starts with: "We won the war in Podrinje but we did not rout the Muslims which we have to do in the forthcoming period. We have to accomplish our final goal which is that Podrinje is entirely Serbian. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa must be militarily defeated." Is this portion of the information unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of it is a military objective, absolutely. And there is a part that could be interpreted twofold. The portion that is questionable to me is the portion referring to the Muslims because there is reference there to Muslims, not to the enemy, because Muslims are civilians, old women, old men, women, children, every one - that's what Muslims is a reference to - as opposed to the earlier portion that we read out where it is very clearly stated that the enemy's life has to be made unbearable, which to me is a fully legitimate military objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see document 65 ter 04191 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a telegram from the Drina Corps command dated the 15th of May, 1995. It is signed by the deputy commander, Colonel Radislav Krstic. In the first paragraph, Mr. Nikolic it says: "According to the information gathered the Muslims are carrying out intense preparations for offensive operations from the general area of Tuzla, Kladanj and the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves," and so on and so forth. Now, please tell me, the term "Muslims are carrying out intense preparations for offensive operations," what is this a reference to? What does the term "Muslims" refer to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a reference to Muslim armed forces in the area mentioned here, including the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04191 receives number D298, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D298 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see the next document in e-court, that's 65 ter 04699.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This document is dated the 19th of July, 1995. It is a document from the Zvornik public security centre and it is signed by the chief of the centre Dragomir Vasic. In the third paragraph he says: "In addition to them, this morning a large group of about 50 Muslims attacked the positions of the Zvornik Brigade in the Pandurica area in an attempt to attempt a breakthrough to reach the Muslim territory." This reference here, where it says, "about 50 Muslims attacked the positions of the Zvornik Brigade," what is it a reference to? Is this a reference to soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a reference to civilians, just as it states there. There is nothing that I should add or comment on. I cannot comment on whatever whoever wrote in their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: According to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, to go through a lot of documents of a military nature and then to ask the witness whether Muslims in that context could be understood as Muslim soldiers is totally useless. It's obvious. It's obvious that in this context, Muslims has limited meaning of Muslim combatants or soldiers or whatever. It's really no use to ask these questions for this purpose. If there is any other purpose, please make it clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to place these documents in context and to add on to the interpretation of the word "Muslims" by this witness and to point out to the witness that the term, "The Muslims" was also a term used to apply to -- to refer to the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I told you a minute ago that, first of all, it's obvious and there is no reason to do that. It's totally superfluous, that it depends on the context. And then to start explaining what you did which was clear to us and which we think is -- and obvious and unnecessary and a waste of time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In relation to this document, are you aware that the assistant commander for morale, assistant commanders for morale, in battalions and companies, as mentioned in this document, were supposed to brief members of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question, whether there is information that the assistant commander briefed personally all the commanders --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, did the command -- the assistant commander for morale did he brief all the members of the brigade on this? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs, that was Major Jevtic, it was not his job to personally brief and to interpret these documents within units. What I can recall is that the battalion commanders were duty-bound to organise meetings where this organisation -- this kind of information would be discussed in their battalions and that Major Jevtic had a supervisory role, in a way. He had to make sure that all of this was implemented in the way that the commander had ordered it. That is what I know for certain about how things were done within brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In this last paragraph it says that the information will be discussed with the assistants within the battalions and as for the units attached to the staff, the person in charge will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have difficulties in finding all this. Are you quoting from a document different from the ones we have on our screens, Mr. Petrusic? Would you please verify?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I didn't pay attention to that. The document should be P1505.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nikolic, did you receive information to the effect that the assistant commander for morale who is responsible for the implementation of this information and for its appropriate interpretation actually did so at the level of the command as suggested in the last paragraph of this information? Could we please see page 3, the last paragraph, 14.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I answered your question for the most part in my previous answer. And just to add, the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs, Major Jevtic, his task was at the level of the Bratunac Brigade command, and that is how it was implemented, as ordered. But as I said a moment ago, the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in English? I think it should be in the second paragraph of paragraph 14, is that correct, because in the first paragraph of paragraph 14 we didn't find that. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At battalion levels, battalions of the Bratunac Brigade, it was not up to Major Jevtic to discuss within those units this information and to brief them on it. That was the task of the battalion commander, so each battalion commander within his own battalion would have an assistant for morale and religious affairs, and they were the ones who would advise and inform each individual soldier of the information within the battalion, and that is the way that the information was dealt with and it was something that every soldier was briefed on, including those who were in positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm trying to get from you is whether you at the command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I think it's time to take a break. Would you also make pauses yourself because your whole next question is already pronounced at a moment when we are still listening to the end of the English translation. Could we first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. We will take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, could you please remember for after the break that questions have to be relevant and clear. We take a break and resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, after this information and you said that this gave a green light for the sniping that was carried out from the area of the Bratunac Brigade on the civilian population in Srebrenica, in other words the border areas, was there anything that you could do on your part to halt these incidents, to stop them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite precise in my evidence. The incidents always existed, even before this information. However, I said that they intensified after this information. The violations of the borders of the enclave and opening fire and not just sniping on the enclave and vice versa, fire coming from the enclave against the Serbian side, intensified after this information. Also, sniping intensified after this information. And as for the send part of your question, I'll answer you now, I did what I could, what was within my powers, to bring this down to sort of acceptable -- to an acceptable framework because you could never stop all incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After your interventions, did those incidents become fewer? Did they abate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not. Because, in spite of my insistence and my going personally to various battalions, the commander ordered at one point that we -- that one part of the soldiers, a number of soldiers, enter the enclave, and we, from the 1st Infantry Battalion and a unit of the military police, we actually entered this area that Ognjenovic demanded. We did that in the morning, in the morning hours, and after that, because the battalion or rather the company refused to move forward, we had to withdraw and remain on the same lines where we had been before. So there was an order from Commander Ognjenovic -- or rather, there were orders issued by Commander Ognjenovic that were in absolute contradiction to all my efforts and also the efforts of many of the officers within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you talk about entering the enclave, the 1st Battalion entering the enclave, what period of time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to the period, perhaps it would be most accurate if I said that this was after the writing and the discussion of this information. Perhaps a month or so later. I can't really recall the exact dates. But I do recall the incidents and I know exactly where this particular incident occurred, not only the incident in the area of the 1st Battalion but also in the area of responsibility of other battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever try to turn to the -- to your superior command in order to resolve these issues, these problems?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever problems I had in that area, where the enclave was violated, fire was opened, there was sniping or anything else, I reported along my chain of command in written form and I informed the security and intelligent organ about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did UNPROFOR lodge any protests with you because of such conduct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If under that we imply their interventions then they were continuously evident whenever the enclave borders were violated or when any issues arose, so they did lodge protests, perhaps even once though I really don't remember the exact time, perhaps once they lodged the protest in writing, in relation to our entrance in violation of the enclave at TT-414, that was in front of the first line of the 1st Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that you will agree with me or agree with the prosecutor that the enclave was armed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The enclave had not been demilitarised, and in the enclave there were forces of the 28th Division which were stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you are in the best position to say whether there were some specific, precise borders of the enclave that were in place.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying this for the sake of the Trial Chamber. I was one of the officers in the commission that went to Potocari on two, three or four occasions, with the task to specifically and precisely define the borders of the enclave, after international forces for the protection of it had entered it, and if you're interested in details, I can talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could it be said that due to those imprecisely established borders, there were some conflicts between the two sides, disputes, that eventually ended as combat operations, disputes about what was whose territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only partly agree with you. One section, the southern section of the enclave, remained contested to the very end. There was never an agreement about it. As for the other parts or sections of the enclave, I'm only talking about the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, mine, that's the sector of Zeleni Jadar and the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. We agreed almost or not almost but rather everything that had to do with the enclave borders. What remained contested was the southern part, a part of Zeleni Jadar where the Serbian side claimed and requested that the UNPROFOR check-point be moved in the direction of Srebrenica about 400 metres in depth, and to set free this road so that the Serbian forces could have a communication between Skelani, Zeleni Jadar and Jasenovo, so that was a part that was not agreed on. And let me add just one more thing. The border of the enclave as agreed and as defined in writing, we endeavoured to adjust that to the facilities that could be found in the field, so we didn't -- oh, I apologise, should I slow down? Yes. We did not have to be physically at the borders of the enclave in order to control certain territory. We used the configuration of the terrain, the dominant features and the borders of the enclave with agreement of the UNPROFOR forces were controlled by fire. Whatever appeared in that section in front of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have to slow down again. If you don't speed up, there is no need to slow down again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will try to abide by that. So we knew exactly where the enclave border was but we did not cover it physically, in the military sense. We covered it from dominant features, dominant points, and by fire. So that we never made any problems, either us or the UNPROFOR. If anyone entered that part of the enclave, which was not possessed by any forces physically, even though fire was opened on it. So that was not the subject of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also had information that a significant part of the Srebrenica enclave in the direction of the Zepa enclave was practically uncovered. It was open for passage; that is to say these two enclaves were practically joined?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree with what you just noted. Never from the moment when Zepa and Srebrenica were declared enclaves were physically -- were they physically separated. Communication between the two enclaves was always possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would you also agree that in accordance to the agreement, these had to be two enclaves on the ground, and in fact they had to be separated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these had to be two enclaves, but I want to make myself absolutely clear. No one prevented us from occupying and closing the ring around the enclaves. Actually I'm talking about the Srebrenica enclave. However, we always had a problem with the lack of forces that we would use to physically and militarily close the circle around the enclave, as it should be done in the military sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And from the north of the enclave, would you agree with me that there were frequent raids and infiltrations aimed both at civilians and the military units of the Drina Corps, from the moment when the enclave came into existence up until July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. You mean the northern part of the Srebrenica enclave? The area of Milici, Visnjica and thereabouts? If so, I would agree with you that in that area, sometimes they would leave, make ambushes, raids and even a military attack on a village that was attacked and torched in that specific period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me that when you talk about the village, that that took place immediately after the attack on Srebrenica by the Drina Corps? Are you talking about June 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember properly, though I wouldn't really allow myself to comment on that, that was in the zone of responsibilities of the Milici brigade so I would ask you to discuss my brigade because I don't know the exact dates, but I do know for sure that the attack on Visnjica which was in the Milici territory was launched before the attack on Srebrenica was launched. I know that for sure but I'm not aware of the details or of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you also said that in the spring, that is to say in April and May, the supply of humanitarian aid or the UNPROFOR convoys and convoys from all other organisations was reduced. My question is this: During those years and immediately before the fall of the enclave, and during the spring of 1995, were there any abuses by those who were supplying the enclave, both with humanitarian aid and also military, logistical support? Was that ever abused by members of the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that there were some abuses but I don't know exactly -- believe me, I have forgotten that. One of the international organisations which was based in Srebrenica did make those abuses, and I know that a vehicle with its cargo was seized from this international organisation because of the abuse, and then the UNHCR also in one instance did abuse its mission, and I know that a truck with goods that they were transporting without an appropriate permit was also seized from them because they tried to smuggle it as part of a convoy into Srebrenica, and please allow me to finish with my answer. But as for the members of UNPROFOR, I do not have any information or any piece of evidence that they abused something and then as a result we took some measures. I really don't know or I don't remember any such instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 14822, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for me to fully understand, did the UNHCR try to smuggle a truck into Srebrenica - is that what you said? - a truck with goods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I said. That's what I said. And the truck was seized, and the -- in regular procedure a report was sent to the command of the Drina Corps, an opinion requested, and they decided that for the time being until the procedure was completed the truck would not be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic you can see one of your documents before you from the 10th of December, 1994, and I think that you just talked about this. The reason why it was seized, or rather, why the convoy was stopped was that it was transporting goods that were not announced or materiel that was not announced. Would you agree with me about this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have not seen this report for quite a long time but I know more or less what it deals with. It was seized because it tried to enter the enclave with goods that were not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the goods that were not allowed, could they be used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you just allow me to look at the document a bit because I don't know what exactly this is about, what was seized and why, so if you can please bear with me a minute. All right. I understand more or less what this is about. Of course, what we see here, the plumbing materials and so on, in fact cannot be connected with the army and its needs but frequently -- or rather, not frequently but there were some situations when some representatives would bring material and try to smuggle it in and it was not under their authority. They were not in charge of organising something like that. Their remit of work was quite different and they had nothing to do with it, so then they told me -- they would say, Yes, we made a mistake. I talked to them personally about this, and their chief admitted that this was not the first time and he said, We tried several times, so if it can pass, fine, if not, never mind. So they accepted that it was their mistake, and they asked me to suspend it and to return to the previous relations that we had so that everything would be decent without any further tensions, so that was the thrust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you what was the quantity of that contraband material, tools and plumbing materials on a whole truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was one vehicle. I'm speaking about specific cases which I think there was no special transport, it was one vehicle, one case, and then in another case it was just one truck that had generators or something that was not permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm now talking about this example. What was it, these plumbing materials? How much was it, what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't remember the quantities anymore in the notification, in the permit. Probably -- actually not probably, I'm sure there were certain quantities and then the inspection it turned out that it was not the quantity from the permit but something else, a different quantity. So the goods were seized. But I don't know off the top of my head exactly which goods were in question and what were the quantities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I understand your last answer to be that plumbing material may have been on the notification, in the permit, but that it might have been more of that? Certain quantities and then the inspection it turned out that it was not the quantity from the permit but something else, a different quantity? Are we talking about still this plumbing materials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would rather tend to say that in the notification, quantities and the type were indicated but I assume that there was something outside of that that was not indicated at all, but was part of the cargo that was being transported. I think that that was probably the case. I'm not quite sure now if they would seize the vehicle -- a vehicle because the quantities deviated. I would say that as part of the plumbing equipment, there was something that was not included in the permit at all. I believe so. But don't hold me to that. I cannot remember that any longer. I assume that that was the reason because I'm the one who wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, before the vehicle reached you, it passed another check-point in Zvornik or, rather, in Karakaj, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on condition that we know where the vehicle was coming from. If it was coming from Serbia, from Belgrade, then what you say would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to say only that at the beginning of the report, this information by you, the Srebrenica-Belgrade route is mentioned, and before that a convoy entered Srebrenica. So if the convoy is going from Belgrade, it would pass through Karakaj and it would also be inspected there. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at your check-point, you would again inspect the convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would be a routine inspection at that check-point as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that it would be impossible to conduct a detailed inspection of the convoys within a reasonable period of time during which the convoys would be expected to be held at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that the time was not limited. You would have as much time as you needed for the inspection. But there was an order which stated that convoys entering would be inspected in detail at the first check-point, all those reaching Srebrenica or entering Srebrenica would already have gone through a detailed check. So since the enclave was formed, the check-point where routine inspections were carried out of convoys and international organisations were -- that was our check-point. That's what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one additional question? MSF which stands for Medecins Sans Frontieres, I think, the medical organisation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Doctors Without Borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if they transported something into the enclave, for whose benefit would that material be used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can answer to that is that material delivered to the enclave would probably marked as being meant for somebody, and I would know that once I saw the documentation. As for the actual distribution of the material, that's something that I don't know. I don't know how it was distributed. I don't know what happened in the enclave. But from the documents, you could see who the material was intended for. Was it for the civilian population in Srebrenica or the medical centre and the hospital in the Srebrenica enclave, this is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it meant to be used in -- well, let's say, treating Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, of course, because that was the only way. There was no other source of medical supplies and material or anything else that had to do with medical assistance. There was no other source, according to my information. That was the only way. And, of course, it included both the population and soldiers, members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They could be treated by that material as well? With that material, I should say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they had to be treated. There was no choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I'm reading the last part of the documents we had on our screen, where it reads: "We particularly draw your attention to the fact that the MSF delegates did not put up resistance or try to make any excuses for their attempt to import into the enclave material that was exclusively meant for Muslims." I have some difficulties in understanding what exactly now they are blamed for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you about what I remember best. So it was either part of the cargo -- well, actually not either. I'm quite sure that they probably had something that was not permitted or something that was not included in the notification where the quantities were indicated. These are the two things that occur to me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Mr. Petrusic, we have to finish in a couple of minutes, so two or three minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, would you agree with me that only what was listed as cargo could enter the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender 14822 to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we decide on that, I would like to ask one final question. Somewhere halfway in the document, Mr. Nikolic, it says: "Through their manipulations and abuse of humanitarian missions, they are selflessly helping the Turks which goes against our interests." What is the reference "Turks," what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is meant are members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or members of the 28th Division who were in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is "Turks" a derogatory term for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14822 receives number D299, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D299 is admitted into evidence. I noticed that the Defence had no problems in presenting a translation in which Turks was explained as derogatory for Muslims, but since there was dispute about it, I thought let's verify with the witness. Mr. Petrusic, I think we are at the time for a break. Could you tell us how much more time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope to be able to finish tomorrow, and there would be enough time for the OTP. Oh, yes, I will try to complete my examination in the course of tomorrow. Perhaps we could go over into the following day, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, we need a bit of time tomorrow morning to start with with an administrative hearing. Second, whether the Chamber will allow you to use the whole of tomorrow or even a portion of the day after that will highly depend on the relevance and the way in which you conduct the cross-examination. The Chamber will carefully monitor that. Could I first instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given or still to be given. Then we would like see you back tomorrow morning. And, Ms. Lindsay, I do understand that you will still be with us tomorrow. Yes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, no loud speaking. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the administrative hearing tomorrow I think it would be in the interests of a productive hearing for the Chamber to have the most current information before it. The latest information the Chamber now has before it is dated the 22nd of May. If the Chamber looks at the last line in that report, it indicates that there was to be another assessment conducted last week. So the Prosecution is requesting the Chamber to inquire with the Registrar whether there is an updated report and whether we could have that some time today to prepare for tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you're invited to provide the Prosecution with any additional information not yet received by it. We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 4th of June, at 9.30 in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of June 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
